blocks.title: 1. Types of Auto Insurance Coverage

challengeCorner.prompt: Explain why a bank requires collision and comprehensive coverage when you finance a car.
hints: The car is collateral for the loan.
Bank wants to ensure it can be repaired or replaced.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Collision and comprehensive are often optional, but lenders require them if you have a car loan. [[imp:Gap insurance covers the difference between the loan balance and the car's value if it's totaled.]]

questions.prompt: The part of auto insurance that covers damage you cause to others is called ___ coverage.
Which coverage pays for a stolen car? (word: liability, collision, or comprehensive)
If you are at fault in a crash, which coverage pays for the other driver's medical bills? (word)

teacherCues: Ask: 'What are the three main parts of an auto insurance policy?'

discoveryHook.scenario: Sara buys a new car and must insure it. Her policy has three major parts: [[kw:liability]] (covers damage she causes to others), [[kw:collision]] (covers damage to her own car in a crash), and [[kw:comprehensive]] (covers non‑crash damage like theft, fire, or hail). Understanding each helps her choose the right coverage.

explanation: [[kw:Auto insurance]] combines several coverages in one policy.
[[kw:Liability coverage]] pays for bodily injury and property damage the insured causes to others. It is usually required by law.
[[kw:Collision coverage]] pays for damage to the insured's own vehicle from a crash, regardless of fault.
[[kw:Comprehensive coverage]] pays for damage from non‑collision events: theft, fire, vandalism, weather, animal strikes.
[[imp:Liability does NOT cover the insured's own injuries or vehicle damage.]]

rows.1: Damage to your car from a crash

visuals.title: Auto Insurance Coverage Types

examples.title: A – Identify coverage type
examples.prompt: A tree falls on your parked car during a storm. Which coverage pays for the damage?

steps: Liability ensures that if you injure someone or damage their property, there is money to compensate them.
Without it, victims might not be able to collect for their losses.
It protects the public, not just the driver.
examples.title: B – Why liability is mandatory
examples.peerPrompt: Think about who pays when an uninsured driver causes an accident.
examples.prompt: Explain why states require drivers to carry liability insurance.

examples.title: C – Collision vs. comprehensive
steps: Hitting an animal is covered under comprehensive, not collision.
Comprehensive covers animal strikes.
examples.prompt: You hit a deer while driving. Is this covered under collision or comprehensive?

questions.prompt: In a split limit policy written as 50/100/25, the first number is the ___ per person limit.
Policy limit 50/100/25. Property damage is $30,000. How much does insurance pay for property damage? (number only, no $)
If per‑accident bodily injury limit is $200,000 and total injuries are $250,000, how much does the insured pay out‑of‑pocket? (number only, no $)

examples.title: A – Apply liability limits
steps: Bodily injury per person: min($60,000, $50,000) = $50,000. Insured owes $10,000 for that person's excess.
Property damage: min($30,000, $25,000) = $25,000. Insured owes $5,000.
Total insurance payment = $75,000.
examples.prompt: Policy limit 50/100/25. An at‑fault accident injures one person with $60,000 medical bills and damages another car worth $30,000. How much does insurance pay?

steps: If you cause a serious accident, damages could exceed low limits.
The injured party can sue you personally for the excess.
High limits protect your assets from being seized.
examples.title: B – Why carry high limits?
examples.peerPrompt: Think about the risk of a lawsuit.
examples.prompt: Explain why someone with significant assets should carry high liability limits.

examples.title: C – Multiple injured
examples.prompt: Policy limit 100/300/50. An accident injures three people: Person A $120,000, Person B $90,000, Person C $80,000. How much does insurance pay for injuries?
steps: Person B: min(90k,100k) = $90,000.
Person C: min(80k,100k) = $80,000.
Total = $270,000, which is within the $300,000 per‑accident limit. So insurance pays $270,000.

teacherCues: Explain the split limit format: e.g., 100/300/50.
100 = bodily injury per person, 300 = total bodily injury per accident, 50 = property damage (in thousands).

notes: Higher limits provide more protection but cost more.
Umbrella policies can provide additional liability coverage above auto limits.
formulaCard.title: Liability Payment with Limits

explanation: Liability limits are often expressed in a [[kw:split limit]] format: $$\text{Bodily Injury per Person / Total Bodily Injury per Accident / Property Damage}$$
The first number is the maximum paid to any one person for injuries.
The second number is the maximum paid for all injuries in one accident.
The third number is the maximum paid for damage to others' property.
[[imp:If damages exceed your limits, you are personally responsible for the excess.]]

rows.2: Maximum for all injured persons in one accident
Damage to others' vehicles or property

visuals.title: Split Limit Example: 100/300/50
visuals.caption: Three separate limits; each applies independently.

confusionCorner.body: The per‑accident bodily injury limit is the total for all injuries in one accident. [[imp:If total injuries exceed that limit, the insurer will not pay more, even if per‑person limits are not exhausted.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: Sara's policy shows liability limits of 100/300/50. This means the insurer will pay up to $100,000 per person for bodily injury, up to $300,000 total for all injuries in one accident, and up to $50,000 for property damage. If she causes a crash with $120,000 in injuries to one person, $100,000 is covered by insurance; she is responsible for the remaining $20,000.

examples.prompt: Collision damage = $2,500, deductible = $500. How much does the insurer pay?
steps: Insurer payment = $2,500 – $500 = $2,000.
Insured pays the first $500.
examples.title: A – Claim with deductible

examples.peerPrompt: Think about premium savings versus out‑of‑pocket risk.
examples.prompt: Explain the trade‑off of choosing a $1,000 deductible over a $250 deductible.
steps: A higher deductible means lower premiums because the insurer assumes less small‑claims risk.
However, if you have a claim, you pay more out‑of‑pocket.
Choose a deductible you can afford if an accident occurs.
examples.title: B – Why choose a higher deductible?

steps: Since $300 < $500, insurer pays $0.
The insured bears the full $300.
examples.title: C – Loss less than deductible

discoveryHook.scenario: Sara has a $500 deductible on collision. She backs into a pole, causing $2,000 damage to her own car. Her insurer pays $2,000 – $500 = $1,500. She pays the first $500. The deductible reduces small claims and keeps premiums lower.

blocks.title: 3. Collision, Comprehensive, and Deductibles

notes: The deductible is subtracted before applying policy limits.
For a total loss, the insurer pays actual cash value minus deductible.
formulaCard.title: Claim Settlement with Deductible

explanation: A [[kw:deductible]] is the amount the insured must pay out‑of‑pocket before the insurer pays for a covered loss.
Collision and comprehensive coverages each have a deductible chosen by the policyholder (e.g., $250, $500, $1,000).
Higher deductible → lower premium, but more out‑of‑pocket if a claim occurs.
Insurer payment = Amount of loss – Deductible (subject to policy limits).
[[imp:Deductibles apply per claim, not per year.]]

visuals.caption: If the loss is less than the deductible, the insurer pays nothing.
visuals.title: Deductible Effect on Claim Payment

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: If the car is totaled, the insurer pays the actual cash value minus the deductible, not the replacement cost. [[imp:Gap insurance can cover the difference if you owe more on a loan than the car's ACV.]]

teacherCues: Explain deductibles: the amount the insured pays before the insurer pays.
Collision and comprehensive each have their own deductible.

examples.peerPrompt: Think about traffic density and crime rates.
examples.prompt: Explain why auto insurance costs more in a big city than in a rural area.
examples.title: B – Why location matters
steps: Urban areas have more traffic, leading to more accidents.
Car theft and vandalism rates are higher.
Repair costs and medical expenses are also typically higher in cities.

examples.prompt: A driver's base premium is $1,200. A speeding ticket adds a 20% surcharge. What is the new premium?
examples.title: C – Calculate premium change

visuals.caption: Many factors are within your control.
visuals.title: Premium Factors and Their Effect

explanation: Auto insurance premiums are based on the insurer's assessment of risk.

Key factors: [[kw:age and gender]] (younger, male drivers pay more), [[kw:driving record]] (accidents and tickets increase premiums), [[kw:location]] (urban areas have higher rates), [[kw:vehicle type]] (expensive or high‑power cars cost more), [[kw:coverage limits and deductibles]] (higher limits raise premiums; higher deductibles lower them).
[[kw:Credit‑based insurance scores]] may also be used in many states.
[[imp:You can lower your premium by maintaining a clean driving record, choosing a higher deductible, and comparing quotes.]]

challengeCorner.prompt: A company charges a base rate of $1,500. A young driver surcharge adds 30%. A multi‑car discount reduces the final premium by 10%. What is the final premium?

confusionCorner.body: Not all factors are equally weighted. [[imp:Your driving record usually has the largest impact on your premium.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

discoveryHook.scenario: Sara's premium quote is higher than her brother's because she's younger, lives in a city with more accidents, and chose lower deductibles. Insurers use many factors to set rates, and understanding them can help you find savings.

formulaCard.title: Claim Payment Summary
notes: For liability claims, the insurer pays the injured party directly.
If the insured is not at fault, their insurer may pay and then subrogate.

explanation: When an insured has a covered loss, the payment depends on the type of coverage, deductibles, and policy limits.
For first‑party coverages (collision, comprehensive): Insurer pays = Loss – Deductible (up to ACV).
For liability (third‑party): Insurer pays the damages the insured is legally liable for, up to policy limits.
[[kw:Subrogation]] is the insurer's right to recover the amount paid from the at‑fault party's insurer.
[[imp:The insured is responsible for amounts exceeding policy limits or deductibles.]]

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: If you are at fault and your liability limits are too low, you may be personally sued for the excess. [[imp:Consider umbrella insurance for extra liability protection.]]

I'll recompute: collision payment = 15,000-500 = 14,500. So insurer pays 25k liability + 14,500 collision = 39,500. Insured pays: excess property 20k + deductible 500 = 20,500. I'll use 25,000, 14,500, 20,500.

If the accident was the other driver's fault, Sara's insurer may recover the $4,500 from the other driver's liability insurance through [[kw:subrogation]].

examples.prompt: You hit a guardrail, causing $3,000 damage to your car. Collision deductible $500. ACV of your car is $10,000. How much does insurance pay?
steps: Insurer payment = $3,000 – $500 = $2,500.
You pay $500.
examples.title: A – Single‑car accident

examples.prompt: Explain what happens if the other driver is at fault and has insurance.
examples.title: B – When the other driver is at fault
steps: You can file a claim with the other driver's liability insurance.
Their insurer should pay for your car repairs and medical bills, up to their limits.
You shouldn't have to pay a deductible (unless you use your own collision coverage for speed).
examples.peerPrompt: Think about who you file a claim with.

examples.prompt: Your car (ACV $8,000) is totaled in a crash. Collision deductible $1,000. How much does your insurer pay?
examples.title: C – Total loss with deductible
steps: Insurer pays ACV – deductible = $8,000 – $1,000 = $7,000.
You receive $7,000.
